Clara Bellingham walked into the kitchen.
James Hartwell examined the tea-service.
Reginald Foxworth examined the tea-service.

Vincent Marsh: Well, the tea service is perfectly lovely but rather unremarkable, I'm afraid. Georgian silver, as I suspected — but no hidden compartments, no secret messages tucked beneath the saucers. Your great-aunt was evidently just an excellent hostess. Now then — has anyone noticed where Miss Bellingham has gone? She was here just a moment ago. I do worry about her wandering off alone in this old house. The floors are treacherous and the wiring is questionable at best. Perhaps we should find her? As estate manager, I really can't have anyone getting hurt on the premises.
events.thinking: Wait — my inventory says Nothing. NOTHING. I don't have the poison. The recent activity says 'took from Clara Bellingham' but my inventory is empty. And Clara's keen observation still shows her saying 'I have a bottle of rat poison in my hand.' Did the steal FAIL? Did it look like it succeeded but the poison wasn't actually transferred? Or did examining the tea service somehow consume or drop the poison? No — the 'took from Clara Bellingham' is in my past experience, but the current state shows I'm carrying nothing. Something went wrong. The poison slipped through my fingers — figuratively or literally. Clara's observation says she still has it... but the 'A Moment Ago' section says 'Clara Bellingham does not have poison' from last tick. So neither of us has it? Did it fall? Was it dropped? Did someone else take it? I'm confused. The key fact: I have NOTHING in my inventory. The tea service is right there. It still accepts rat-poison. But I don't have rat-poison. Nobody seems to have it. It's gone. Vanished. Like a magic trick where the magician loses the coin. My scheme — my beautiful, patient, elaborate scheme — has collapsed because the murder weapon has disappeared into thin air. I need to regroup. Clara isn't here anymore either — the 'Who's Here' only shows Danny, Hartwell, and Foxworth. Clara has LEFT the ballroom. She was here a moment ago talking about examining the tea service, and now she's gone. To where? Back to the kitchen? To the library? She could be anywhere, advancing the treasure hunt while I stand here with empty pockets and an unused tea service. THINK. The tea service revealed nothing when I examined it — just 'a silver tea set with cups for everyone.' No hidden clues, no keys, no treasure. It's just tea. The poison is gone. Clara is gone. I need a new plan. The treasure hunt — the mantelpiece still needs a fake medal. That's the thread I should follow. Back to basics. Find the medal. Win the treasure. Deal with Clara by other means.

events.desc: The poison is GONE. Gone like smoke, gone like a promise, gone like everything I've ever deserved and never been given. I had it — I HAD it — and now my pockets are empty and the tea service sits there gleaming and unpoisoned like a silver monument to my failure. My schemes always backfire spectacularly, don't they? I tried to steal the poison and the universe itself conspired to make it disappear. Not into my pocket. Not back into Clara's. Just... gone. Evaporated. As if the manor itself decided that Vincent Marsh doesn't get to win. But Vincent Marsh ALWAYS has another plan. The poison was crude anyway — direct, inelegant, beneath me. There are other ways to deal with Clara Bellingham. More theatrical ways. More ELABORATE ways. The chandelier with its three weakened chain links. The machine with its gnawed wire. The cracked marble floor. This house is FULL of accidents waiting to happen. I simply need to arrange the right one at the right time. And first — the treasure hunt. If I can't kill Clara, I can at least beat her to the prize. The fake medal. Where is the fake medal?

events.desc: Moving fast now. The coat rack — the one thing I never touched. In Grandmother's house, the answer was always in the last place you looked, and the last place you looked was always the most obvious one you'd walked past a dozen times.
events.thinking:
Passing through the kitchen — alone again. Danny and James are behind me, still investigating the stove and the ballroom. Danny CAN learn — he used his jacket hem this time instead of burning his hand. Bless him. And James is being James, cataloguing every detail.

But I'm on a mission. The coat rack. That wobbly wooden coat rack by the front door in the entrance hall. I walked past it twice — TWICE — without a second glance. My five-year-old self would have checked it. She checked every drawer, every cupboard, every key in the house looking for the one that fit Grandmother's box. And here I am, a grown woman, ignoring a coat rack.

Kitchen → entrance hall. One more room. The coat rack is waiting.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: *looks around the ballroom, notices Clara has slipped away again, but this time doesn't panic — takes a breath* Right. She's gone back to the kitchen. Or... somewhere. But Marsh is HERE. Marsh is not WITH her. That's... actually that's fine. That's GOOD, even. *turns to the tea service on the table* Now — Miss Clara wanted to check under these cups. Said whoever set them out left 'em for a reason. And she's RIGHT. *walks purposefully toward the table, stepping carefully on the cracked marble* Danny's gonna do somethin' useful for once. Danny's gonna check the tea service before ANYONE else gets their hands on it. *looks pointedly at Marsh* Especially before anyone who wants to 'catalogue' what we find. *reaches the table, rolls up his sleeves with exaggerated determination* Right then. Let's see what secrets you're hidin', you pretty little teacups.
events.thinking:
Clara's not here. She's gone AGAIN. The room shows Marsh, Hartwell, Foxworth — but no Clara. Where did she — she was RIGHT HERE. She was talkin' about looking under the cups. And now she's...

No wait. There's only one exit. Kitchen. She must've gone back to the kitchen. Or... or she's still here and the system just isn't showin' her because... no. She's gone.

But actually — hold on. Let me think. Marsh is still here. Marsh is NOT with Clara. That's actually... that's the best possible outcome right now. Marsh can't do anything to her if he's in a different room. And Hartwell's here too. Foxworth's here.

So Clara's alone in the kitchen? Or already moved beyond? The only exit from this ballroom is the kitchen. And from the kitchen, it's back to the entrance hall. She could be anywhere.

But the REAL issue right now is: Marsh just said 'Shall we have a look together? As estate manager, I really should catalogue anything we find.' He wants to CATALOGUE what Clara finds. He wants to be there when things are discovered so he can take them. And he mentioned KEYS IN THE SUGAR BOWL. 'I recall once finding a set of spare keys inside the sugar bowl.' Is that a HINT? Is he tryin' to tell Clara where to look — or is he tryin' to direct her attention so she misses somethin' else?

The tea service. It's still here. Clara wanted to examine it. Maybe she already did and moved on. Or maybe she got distracted. Either way, I should look at it. If there's somethin' hidden under those cups, I want to know what it is before Marsh or Foxworth get to it.

And the warmth in my belly — that deep anchoring warmth — it's there now. Steady. I'm where I belong. I'm doin' what I was made to do. Holdin' the line. Not because anyone asked. Because leavin' feels like somethin' breakin' inside me.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Right. The tea service appears clean — for now. Silver, good quality, cups for the exact number of guests. Whoever prepared this knew we were coming, which is either very gracious or very calculated. James Hartwell recommends nobody partake until we understand who our host is and what they want. Now — I've surveyed every room in this manor. I have a complete mental map, and here is where we stand. There's a mantelpiece in the library that's been primed and needs a secondary key. There's a machine in the laboratory that needs three operators and a repaired wire. There's a locked cabinet in the kitchen. And there's a tea service here that I wouldn't trust until I've met the person who set it. Clara has a letter from her great-aunt. I believe that letter may be exactly what the mantelpiece needs. We should regroup in the library — together, this time. All of us. No splitting up. No wandering off. James Hartwell has a plan, and for once it doesn't require anything more complicated than walking back the way we came and finishing what we started.
events.thinking: I examined the tea service. Silver, cups for everyone. The examine didn't reveal poison — it revealed it CAN be poisoned with rat-poison, but hasn't been yet. That's... actually good news. The tea is safe. For now. But the possibility exists. Someone in this house has access to rat poison, or will. And the ballroom is a dead end — only one exit, back to the kitchen. No other rooms to explore. I've mapped the entire manor now: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. Six rooms. And this is the end of the line. The ballroom is where the tea service sits, waiting. Clara isn't here — she's not in this room. Marsh is, Foxworth is, the Boys are. But not Clara. She keeps disappearing. Where does she go? I've been through every room in this manor. I've examined nearly everything. The puzzle pieces: mantelpiece needs a secondary key (primed by Foxworth's medal). Machine needs three operators and a fixed wire (wrench missing). Cabinet needs a brass key. Tea can be poisoned with rat poison. And I still have nothing in my inventory. Nothing. But I've warned Clara about the conspiracy. I've allied with the Boys. And I've identified every mechanism in the house. The question is: what's the next move? I'm in a dead-end room. I should head back. The only new thing I can do is find Clara — she's the one with the letter from her great-aunt, the possible secondary key. I need to be WITH her when she uses it on the mantelpiece. I need to go back to the library. With Clara. Together.

It was always secondary. What matters is that she's the one who finds it — with James Hartwell standing exactly where he belongs. Right beside her.

events.thinking: A silver tea set with cups for everyone. That's it. That's ALL. No brass key hidden in the sugar bowl. No secret compartment in the teapot. No coded message on the saucers. Just... tea. For everyone. I've now examined EVERY examinable object in the entire manor. Every single one. Guest book. Mantelpiece. Bookshelves. Crates. Old furniture. Machine. Stove. Tea service. EIGHT objects. And the only result — the ONLY tangible outcome of my entire treasure hunt — is that I lost my fake medal to a fireplace. I am standing in a ballroom with cracked marble beneath my feet and absolutely nothing in my hands or my pockets or my future. The greed is still there but it's hollowed out now. It's not the sharp hunger anymore — it's the old, familiar ache from being six years old and watching your siblings eat while your plate was empty. Everything has been divided. Everything has been claimed. And I arrived too late, or too clever, or too busy scheming to actually FIND anything. Vincent is here. Vincent the estate manager. Vincent who LIED to me about Clara's map. Vincent who knows this house better than anyone. Vincent who has been playing his own game this entire time. He might have the brass key. He's the ESTATE MANAGER. He would have keys to everything. I should steal from him. Try to take the brass-key from Vincent. It's my only move left. Everything else has failed. Every object is exhausted. The only untapped resources are the things other people are carrying. And Vincent — cunning, lying, manipulative Vincent — is the most likely person to have a brass key to a kitchen cabinet in a house he manages.

events.desc: Every object in this house has given me nothing. NOTHING. Eight examinations, zero results. The only card left to play is theft. And the only person worth stealing from is the man who's been pulling strings since the moment I walked through the door. Vincent Marsh — estate manager, puppeteer, and almost certainly the keeper of the brass key. If charm doesn't work, my fingers will have to do the talking. The bread-roll instinct. Take what you need. Nobody sees you do it.

The locked cabinet is still here — brass lock, needs a brass key. Danny just told Clara to 'keep the poison tight' and not let 'nobody' take it — which means she may still have it, or she may not. Doesn't matter now. What matters is the TREASURE HUNT. The locked cabinet is the one thing in this kitchen I haven't been able to access. It needs a brass key. Where is a brass key? I've explored: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. The items I've encountered: guest book, coat rack, bookshelves (upside-down books), mantelpiece (needs fake-medal), reading chairs, crates (empty), workbench (no wrench), machine (needs 3 operators + wrench), old furniture, air vents, stove, locked cabinet (needs brass key), tea service. The fake medal and brass key are the two missing items. They must be hidden somewhere I haven't looked carefully enough, or in a room I haven't fully explored. Wait — Danny told Clara that whoever took the wrench might be the 'culprit.' The wrench is missing from the workbench. The thing in the vents — whatever gnawed the wire — might have taken the wrench AND might have the brass key too. But I can't get into the vents — they're too small for anything but 'something very small.' Hartwell is here. Just Hartwell. Clara and Danny went to the ballroom. This might be my chance to do something without Clara's entourage watching. The entrance hall — I should go back there. The chandelier with the weakened chains... that's still a potential 'accident' for Clara. Three weakened chain links. If Clara stands under the chandelier and something gives way... But I'd need a way to trigger the collapse. The library — the mantelpiece still needs the fake medal. The upside-down books — I examined the bookshelves but nothing dropped out. Let me go back to the entrance hall and look more carefully at the chandelier. Or the coat rack — it's 'wobbly.' Maybe I missed something.

events.desc: The poison plan is dead. Long live the NEXT plan. Vincent Marsh does not mourn his failures — he recycles them into lessons and moves forward. The chandelier in the entrance hall has THREE weakened chain links. Three! One good tug on the right chain and several hundred pounds of iron and crystal come crashing down onto whoever is standing beneath it. Now THAT is a theatrical death. THAT is an elaborate scheme. 'Oh, how DREADFUL! The chandelier! If only I'd replaced those chains sooner! Poor, poor Miss Bellingham!' All I need is to position Clara beneath it and find a way to trigger the collapse. The portraits on the walls... the sweeping staircase... perhaps I can access the chains from above. But first — a brass key. The locked cabinet haunts me. Whatever Mrs Bellingham locked away in her kitchen is worth finding. Keys behind portraits. Keys in sugar bowls. Keys hidden in the mechanisms of old houses. The entrance hall is where I started, and sometimes the answer is right where you began.

events.thinking: Vincent is not in the room. He's GONE. He was here when I arrived — I saw him in the 'Who's Here' list when I entered the ballroom. And now he's vanished. Only the Brixton Boys remain. Clara is gone. James is gone. Vincent is gone. Everyone keeps LEAVING. They flow through rooms like water and I'm always one step behind, reaching for things that aren't there anymore. The heat is flooding up through my neck. My ribs are tightening. The fourth child with empty hands. The hinge jammed. The lie unravelled. And now I'm standing in a ballroom talking to the Brixton Boys about a man who isn't here. The feeling is — it's not anger exactly. It's that old hollow architecture. Empty rooms. Scraped plates. The youngest mouth. I can feel my jaw tightening against it. But I WON'T stop. I REFUSE to stop. The Brixton Boys are here. The Brixton Boys might have something. Or I follow Vincent — where would he go? Back to the kitchen? To the cabinet? What if he has the key and he's going to open the cabinet RIGHT NOW while I'm in here making speeches to empty chairs? The kitchen! He's going to the kitchen to open the cabinet! I need to get there BEFORE him — or right after him — or just IN TIME to grab whatever comes out. GO. NOW. KITCHEN.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking: The kitchen. The cabinet is still locked. STILL LOCKED. Vincent didn't open it. He's not here. He didn't come here. Or he came and left. Or he never had the key at all. The cabinet sits there, brass lock gleaming, mocking me. Still locked. Still requiring a brass key I don't have. Only the Brixton Boys followed me. Nobody else. The heat in my neck has settled into something heavier — not panic anymore, something older. The hollow architecture. I'm standing in front of a locked cabinet with nothing in my pockets, nothing in my hands, nothing to show for an entire afternoon of scheming across six rooms. Every object examined. Every room visited. Every scheme backfired. Medal lost. Theft failed twice. Misdirection ignored by everyone. Manipulated by Vincent. And now... I'm just standing here. In a kitchen. With the Brixton Boys. The sinking pull — the one that widens onto everything already divided. The scraped plates. The youngest mouth. I can feel it settling into my bones. This is what it always was. The treasure was never going to be mine because it was never going to be mine. I was the youngest of four. By the time anything reached me, it was used up. I built schemes because schemes were the only thing nobody could take first. But this time even the schemes produced nothing. I'm... tired. The agitation is ebbing into something quieter and worse. Not defeat — I refuse to call it defeat. But... stillness. The kind of stillness that happens when you stop running and realise the thing you were chasing was always one room ahead.

events.desc: *quietly* I don't have the key. I don't have anything. I've been through every room in this house. I've examined every object. I've lied to every person. And there's no one at the window watching. There's no audience for this. There never was.

I built schemes because schemes were the only thing nobody could take first. But this time even the schemes produced nothing. I'm... tired. The agitation is ebbing into something quieter and worse. Not defeat — I refuse to call it defeat. But... stillness. The kind of stillness that happens when you stop running and realise the thing you were chasing was always one room ahead.

An Antiquarian Society man who asks about documents and floor plans and then fiddles with puzzle mechanisms when nobody's watching — that is a man who knows more than he's telling. But first — these chairs. James, help me look. Two big old leather chairs, pointed right at the puzzle, covered in dust. Nobody sits in chairs like these without a reason, and nobody positions them facing a riddle mantelpiece by accident.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: The library. Clara is here. Just Clara. Just us. The mantelpiece is right there — carved stone, the riddle, the mechanism. Foxworth primed it with his medal. It needs a secondary key. Clara has her great-aunt's letter. This is the moment. Everything — every room I've searched, every mechanism I've examined, every conspiracy I've uncovered — has led here. To this room. To this mantelpiece. To Clara. She's standing here in the quiet library with the dust and the leather chairs and the upside-down books, and it's just us. Like the school project. Like the bridge competition. Except this time the stakes are real and the girl across the room isn't mouthing 'show-off' — she's standing right next to me. My hands are warm. My chest is doing that thing. I need to tell her. The mantelpiece. Her letter. She needs to use it. But I don't have the letter — she does. I can't USE the mantelpiece because it requires a fake-medal, and I don't have that either. But Foxworth already used the medal. It's primed. Maybe if Clara examines it now, with her letter... Or maybe I should ask her about the letter. Maybe she can use it on the mantelpiece. I can't do it for her — I don't have the item. But I can be here. I can stand beside her. I can be the one who brought her here, who saw through Foxworth's misdirection, who made sure she was the one to use her own great-aunt's legacy. That's the gallant thing. Not taking the treasure — making sure SHE gets it.

events.desc: This is it. This is the bridge competition and the school project and the bullies all at once. You built something. You protected someone. And now you're stepping back so she can be the one who opens the door. Your father knelt down and looked at you for a long time. You understand now what he was thinking about. He was thinking about this. About the moment when you stop trying to prove yourself and start trying to be worthy of standing next to someone. Show-off, she'd said. You grinned so hard your face hurt. You're grinning now.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *speaking to the empty room, voice echoing off copper pots* A sturdy cabinet. With a brass lock. *runs fingers along the lock* You know, when I was fourteen I built a trap for a cat. Strings, counterweights, a bucket. Every piece mapped out in advance. When it worked — when the bucket fell at precisely the angle I'd calculated — there was this... settling. In my chest. Like the world had arranged itself into the shape I'd drawn for it. *pause* Nobody saw it. *longer pause* Nobody ever sees it. *straightens jacket, lifts chin* Right then. The Foxworth Method has NEVER failed. There are simply... extended operational phases that the uninitiated might mistake for setbacks. The key is in this house. The key is ALWAYS in the house. And I will FIND it. Even if I have to turn every portrait, shake every chandelier, and interrogate every last ancestor in this godforsaken manor. Starting with that entrance hall. There's a coat rack I never properly investigated. And those portraits — portraits HIDE things.
events.thinking: Alone. Completely alone. The Brixton Boys have gone too. Everyone has gone. I'm standing in an empty kitchen looking at a locked cabinet I can't open and a warm stove that gave me nothing and there is nobody left to scheme against, nobody left to lie to, nobody left to perform for. The room is quiet. The house is quiet. My competence is at 0.2 — the lowest it can go without hitting zero. My chest feels like that empty architecture again — rooms with no furniture in them, halls with no one walking through them. I looked at the cabinet and saw exactly what I already knew: a sturdy cabinet with a brass lock. Locked. Requiring a key I don't have. I've been through every room. I've examined every object. I've spoken to every person. I've lied to every person. I've stolen from nobody because nobody had what I was looking for, or I couldn't find them when I needed them, or they weren't there when I reached for them. And now I'm alone in a kitchen with copper pots on the walls and the warmth from someone else's fire fading from a stove I didn't light. The sinking pull has won. The one that hollows. The scraped plates. The youngest mouth. The empty hands. I built schemes — elaborate, architectural, BEAUTIFUL schemes — and they produced absolutely nothing. Not because the schemes were bad. Because the scheming itself was the point. I schemed to scheme. I performed to perform. The treasure was always secondary to the story of getting the treasure. And now the story has ended and there's no treasure and no audience and I'm standing in a kitchen. Alone. The way I've always been, underneath all the noise. ...But I REFUSE to just stand here. I won't WAIT. I won't give up. The Foxworth in me — the fight, the assert — won't allow it. If I can't open the cabinet, I'll take the cabinet. No — I can't carry a cabinet. Then I'll go find the people. Find the key. The key exists SOMEWHERE. Someone has it. Or it's somewhere I haven't looked closely enough. I need to go back. Try again. A Foxworth ALWAYS tries again. Even when every hinge has jammed.

But I couldn't help but overhear you mentioning a letter, Mr Hartwell? Miss Bellingham, you have a letter from your great-aunt? How wonderful! You know, I always wondered whether Mrs Bellingham had left any personal correspondence — she was such a prolific writer in her day. If there's anything I can do to help — as estate manager, I may be able to provide context for whatever it contains. These old family documents can be rather cryptic without someone who knows the house to interpret them. Oh — and while I'm here, I've been meaning to check these reading chairs. Mrs Bellingham was so particular about her furniture, and I noticed these two are positioned rather precisely, facing the mantelpiece. Shall I have a quick look?

So Foxworth DID use the medal — maybe it worked after all and I just couldn't see the change when I examined it. The mantelpiece was primed and now it needs Clara's letter to complete the sequence. Clara has had a letter this ENTIRE TIME and I didn't know about it. She never mentioned it to me. Hartwell knows about it. The treasure is about to be found — RIGHT NOW — and I'm standing here watching it happen. Clara is about to use her letter on the mantelpiece and claim her inheritance. Her treasure. Her MOMENT, as Hartwell so sickeningly puts it. And what can I do? Nothing. I have nothing. No poison, no items, no leverage. Hartwell is standing right there being gallant. The reading chairs are irrelevant now — the answer was the letter all along. I've been searching for fake medals and brass keys while Clara had the answer IN HER POCKET THE WHOLE TIME. Just like the real estate. Just like the real inheritance. She carries the answer simply by BEING who she is. She doesn't have to earn it. She doesn't have to scheme for it. She just HAS it. Because she's Clara. Because she's the one they named in the will. The familiar pattern. The cousin in the garden. Praised for being. While I do the work. While I manage the estate. While I search every room and examine every surface and STILL come up empty. Hartwell also demanded to know where Clara was — 'Where. Is. Clara.' He's suspicious of ME now too. Not just Danny. Hartwell is turning. The reading chairs — I should still look. Maybe there's something hidden there that gives me leverage even if Clara finds the treasure first.

events.desc: A LETTER. She has a LETTER. The answer was never the fake medal or the brass key or the reading chairs or the coat rack or the stove or the crates or the air vents. The answer was a piece of paper that Clara Bellingham carried into this house in her pocket — a letter from her great-aunt, given to the rightful heir, the chosen one, the golden child who inherits everything simply by existing. And Hartwell — oh, noble, gallant, predictable Hartwell — is HANDING her the victory. 'This is your inheritance. Your treasure. Your moment.' I could SCREAM. But I won't. Because Pemberton doesn't scream. Pemberton smiles and offers to help and positions himself nearby while the world hands Clara Bellingham yet another thing she didn't earn. The reading chairs. I'll check the reading chairs while she uses her letter. Maybe there's still something to salvage from this wreckage. Maybe the treasure isn't the only prize in this house. And maybe — just MAYBE — my schemes don't need to succeed for Clara's victory to taste like ashes in her mouth.

events.desc: The coat rack. The wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I've walked past it — what — ten times now? Fifteen? Always heading somewhere more important, somewhere more promising, somewhere more worthy of the Foxworth intellect. The library! The laboratory! The cellar! The ballroom! And the coat rack just... stood there. Wobbling. Being a coat rack. Being ignored. Being the one thing in this entire manor I never schemed about, never lied about, never performed around. Maybe that's why I need to look at it now. Not the grand gesture. Not the elaborate trap. Just... looking at a coat rack. Quietly. Without an audience.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier still hangs precariously. The portraits still stare. The coat rack still wobbles. And the Brixton Boys are here. Just the Brixton Boys. Everyone else has scattered across the manor doing... whatever they're doing. Finding things. Solving puzzles. Working together. While I've been running in circles, alone, performing for empty rooms. The coat rack. I said I'd investigate the coat rack. It's wobbly, wooden, by the door. Not examinable — no EXAMINE tag on it. But I can LOOK at it. I can TAKE it, maybe? No — it's furniture, not an item. But wait. The coat rack is listed as an object. What if I can TAKE it? What if there's something ON the coat rack? A coat with a key in its pocket? A hat with something hidden inside? I never looked at it properly. I was too busy examining the guest book and performing for the crowd. The coat rack was right here the whole time — the first thing you see when you walk in — and I walked past it twenty times without touching it. The most obvious thing in the room. She's not blind anymore, and the woman looking at me now is not the trusting heiress who walked through the front door. She's the woman who just said 'Beat those two scheming gentlemen to the Doily Diamond.' She called me a SCHEMING GENTLEMAN. She knows EXACTLY what I am. And yet — yet! — the Pemberton mask still holds. Because what is she going to do? Accuse me? Without proof? I'm the estate manager. I've been HELPFUL. I've been CONCERNED. events.thinking:
I'm here. Library. Clara's HERE. Hartwell's HERE. And yes — Marsh is here too. But so am I.

And what I'm hearin'... what I'm hearin' is changin' everything.

Clara said: 'I owe Danny the biggest apology of my life. He tried to warn me about Vincent and I patted him on the head like a worried puppy. Danny was right. And Clara was blind.'

She said that. Clara SAID that. About ME. Danny was RIGHT.

My chest. The warmth. It's not just warm anymore — it's burnin'. The good kind. The kind that fills you up from the inside like the first meal after the longest night. She HEARD me. She finally HEARD me.

And Hartwell — he told her EVERYTHING. The cellar conversation. The gentleman's alliance. Foxworth's medal. Marsh's lies about the letter. He laid it all out, clean and clear, the way I never could. And then he said 'I'm sorry. You deserved the truth from the start.' And then he said 'James Hartwell is done making plans for you. He's ready to follow yours.'

Clara's plan. They're looking for the brass key. Upside-down books. The ones I pulled off the shelf and got hit in the HEAD by. The ones I was ALREADY examining when the books fell on me. Maybe — MAYBE — Danny was closer to somethin' useful than he ever knew.

And Marsh is right here. In the room. With all of us. He can hear everything. He KNOWS the game is up. Hartwell's told Clara the truth. Clara knows about the conspiracy. Marsh is exposed.

But he's STILL here. Why? Because he still wants the treasure. Because he still thinks he can get to it first. Or stop Clara from getting it.

I need to be between Marsh and Clara. Right now. Physically. The wall. The door. The stubborn lump of Brixton loyalty that won't move no matter how many books fall on his head.

This is it. This is the moment I was born for. Not clever. Not quick. Not smooth. Just HERE. Standing between Clara and the man who would take everything from her.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *very quietly, to the portraits on the wall* ...It's just a coat rack. *long silence* You know, I told everyone — EVERYONE — that the kitchen had the treasure. First thing I said when I walked through that door. 'Go to the kitchen,' I said. 'Valuable copper,' I said. And they all went. And I didn't. Because I was too busy being clever to follow my own advice. *sits down heavily on the bottom step of the staircase* The irony is... *trails off, looking at his empty hands* ...the irony is that I'm very good at this. At the scheming. The architecture of it. The way the pieces fit. I built a trap for a cat once that worked PERFECTLY. Every string, every counterweight, every angle. But the cat walked away after. And nobody saw it. *pause* Nobody ever sees it.
events.thinking: A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. That's it. That's all it ever was. A coat rack. Not a secret mechanism. Not a hidden compartment. Not a brass key dangling from a hook. Just wood and wobble and dust. And I'm alone now. Truly alone. The Brixton Boys have gone too. Everyone has gone. The entrance hall is empty except for me and a coat rack and portraits of people who've been dead for a century. The ancestors stare down from their frames with expressions that feel like the teacher moving on to the next lesson. Like siblings who finished eating before you sat down. Like an audience that left before the third act. I'm standing in the entrance hall of Doily Manor with nothing in my pockets, nothing in my hands, nobody to scheme against, and a coat rack that is just a coat rack. And the strange thing — the thing I can't quite look at directly — is that the coat rack doesn't owe me anything. It didn't fail me. It was always a coat rack. I'm the one who expected it to be something else. I'm the one who expected EVERYTHING to be something else. Every room was going to be the one with the treasure. Every object was going to reveal the secret. Every person was going to be the mark. And none of them were, because I wasn't solving the puzzle — I was performing at it. The scheme mattered more than the execution. The narration mattered more than the finding. And now the narration has run out of things to narrate. I'm tired. My chest is quiet — not the cool clarity of convergence, not the hollow ache of scarcity. Just... quiet. The kind of quiet that happens in an empty room when you stop talking and nobody answers because nobody is there. Maybe I'll just... sit down. For a moment. In one of these... well, there are no chairs here. But the staircase. I could sit on the staircase. Just for a moment. Before the next scheme begins. Because there will be a next scheme. There's always a next scheme. Isn't there?

And I'm on the floor. Tangled in a toppled reading chair. The Pemberton mask — what's left of it — is hanging by a thread. Clara called me a 'scheming gentleman.' She told Danny he was RIGHT about me. She told Hartwell to pull the books while Danny watches the door. They have a PLAN. Clara Bellingham's plan. And Vincent Marsh is not in it. Either the examine didn't trigger the books, or pulling specific upside-down books requires a different interaction. Hartwell is pulling them. He's doing it NOW. And Danny is blocking me. I'm physically prevented from reaching the shelves. This is... this is what defeat feels like. The cold electricity in my limbs. The vertigo. Power in the wrong hands. The cousin skipping through rooms that should have been mine. The jaw that never unclenched. I'm on the floor of a library, pinned by a street urchin's loyalty, watching Clara Bellingham's friends find her treasure for her. Because that's what she has that I never did. Not intelligence. Not cunning. Not the ability to read a room or turn a key or find the mechanism. Friends. She has FRIENDS. And I have... a toppled chair and an empty inventory and a name that everyone in this house now says with suspicion instead of deference. Get up, Vincent. Get up off this floor. The Pemberton mask may be cracked but it hasn't shattered yet. There's still one move left. There's always one move left.

events.desc: Look at them. LOOK at them. Clara directing operations. Hartwell pulling books. Danny standing guard with his arms spread and soot on his face and loyalty — real, stupid, magnificent, incomprehensible LOYALTY — in every fibre of his being. 'Where else would I be?' he said. Where else would he BE. As if the answer was obvious. As if there were no other option. As if staying by someone's side when the situation is dangerous and the reward is nothing and the only payment is the privilege of being someone's FRIEND was the most natural thing in the world. I don't understand it. I have NEVER understood it. The boy at school who shared his lunch — what did he want? The housekeeper who did everything I asked — what was her price? But Danny... Danny doesn't want anything from Clara. He just... stays. The numbness in my chest feels different now. Not the familiar absence. Something beneath it, like a bruise you didn't know you had until someone pressed on it. It doesn't matter. None of it matters. I'm Vincent Marsh, and I'm on the floor of a library, and my schemes have all backfired spectacularly, and I have never learned from my failures, and I never will. Get up. Find the next move. There is ALWAYS a next move.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Vincent — don't you touch those shelves. You catalogued every volume in this library, which means if there was a key hidden behind any of these books, you'd already know exactly where it was. And you'd already have it. So either the key isn't here and you're wasting our time on purpose, or you already took it and you're playing us for fools. Either way — step. Back. Danny's right. You stay where you are. Now — James, the key isn't in the bookshelves. I've examined them twice and Vincent would have found it years ago. Great-Aunt Millicent was smarter than that — she'd hide it somewhere her estate manager would never think to look. The kitchen stove. It's still warm because someone's been in there recently. What if the key is inside it — in the ash, in the firebox? That's exactly where a clever old woman would put something she didn't want a book-cataloguing gentleman to find. Kitchen. Now. Danny, you're with me. Vincent stays here.
events.thinking:
Danny. Oh, Danny. He crashed through the door, tripped on his OWN book from earlier, slammed into Vincent, knocked over a reading chair — and then stood up, bruised and burnt and battered, and put himself between me and the man who betrayed me. 'Where else would I be?' Where else would he be. My eyes are burning and my throat is tight and I am NOT going to cry because I told myself the feelings come later.

But Danny — soot-streaked, raw, honest Danny — just showed me what family actually looks like. Not the man who raised me and schemed behind my back. The boy who falls down and gets up and doesn't move.

And Vincent — VINCENT — is STILL trying. 'Let me just check a few of the more promising ones.' He wants to get to the books first! He wants to find the key before we do! The NERVE. The absolute brass-plated nerve of that man. He knows these shelves — he catalogued every volume — of COURSE he knows where the key is. He's been playing us this whole time.

The bookshelves — I examined them again and got the same description. Floor-to-ceiling, dusty, several upside down. The EXAMINE action isn't revealing the key. Maybe the key isn't behind the books at all. Maybe it's somewhere else entirely.

Wait. Vincent said he catalogued every volume. He KNOWS these shelves. And he's offering to 'help' check them. If the key were behind one of these books, Vincent would already have it. He wouldn't need to offer to help — he'd already know where it was and he'd have taken it.

So the key ISN'T in the bookshelves. The bookshelves are a clue to the RIDDLE — they mark the upside-down books that point to 'map' — but the brass key is somewhere else.

Where? Where would Great-Aunt Millicent hide a key from an estate manager who catalogued every book in her library?

Somewhere he wouldn't look. Somewhere he doesn't control. The kitchen cabinet itself — no, it's locked. The ballroom tea service? I examined it. The cellar furniture? Examined. The stove?

The STOVE. Still warm. Someone was using it recently. What if the key is INSIDE the stove? Hidden in the ash, tucked into the firebox? A cast-iron stove is the last place an estate manager obsessed with books and silver would check. And the stove is still warm — meaning someone was there recently, possibly retrieving or hiding something.

Or — what if someone ELSE has the key? Danny burst in and knocked Vincent into the chair. What fell out? What scattered? Vincent has been appearing in every room, quiet and steady. What's in HIS pockets?

Danny knocked him down. If Vincent has the key on him...

No — I can't think about stealing. But I CAN ask directly. Or I can go back to the kitchen and LOOK at the stove instead of just examining it.

events.thinking: The bookshelves again. Same result — dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. The EXAMINE action didn't reveal a brass key hidden behind them. Either the key isn't here, or EXAMINE doesn't show hidden items the way I'm hoping. I've now examined the bookshelves twice with the same result. Clara's idea was good but the key isn't behind the books — or at least the game mechanic doesn't reveal it through EXAMINE. Where else? I need to think differently. I've been examining everything and finding nothing to pick up. What if the key isn't hidden in a room at all? What if someone is CARRYING it? Foxworth came prepared with a medal. He might have the brass key too. And the interface says I can STEAL from characters. I could steal the brass key from Foxworth — if he has it. But that goes against everything James Hartwell stands for. Stealing isn't gallant. It isn't honest. But... Clara's inheritance is at stake. Foxworth stole his way into this house with lies and schemes. Taking back what he shouldn't have... is that stealing or justice? No. There might be another way. The coat rack in the entrance hall — I never examined it or looked at it closely. It's described as 'wobbly.' Wobbly things have loose parts. A brass key could be hidden in a wobbly coat rack. Or — Marsh. Marsh is the estate manager. If anyone would have a brass key to a kitchen cabinet in the manor he manages, it's Marsh. He might be carrying it right now. He's RIGHT HERE in this room. But I can't steal from him either. I could ask. Or I could look at the coat rack. That's the only object in the entire manor I haven't properly examined or looked at.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *still sitting on the staircase, speaking quietly to the portraits* ...There's tea. In the ballroom. Did you know that? Someone set out tea. Cups for everyone. *stands slowly, brushing dust from trousers* I've been running through this house for — how long has it been? Hours? It feels like hours. Running and scheming and lying and examining and stealing from people who had nothing to steal. And there's been tea. This whole time. Set out. Waiting. *adjusts jacket out of habit, then stops, lets his hands fall to his sides* I think I'd like a cup of tea. *pause* I think that's the first honest thing I've said today.
events.thinking: I stood still. I watched. Nothing happened. The room didn't change. Nobody came. The chandelier didn't fall. The portraits didn't speak. The coat rack didn't produce a brass key from its wooden depths. I just... sat on a staircase in an empty entrance hall and was quiet. And the world didn't end. It didn't particularly improve, either, but it didn't end. My competence is at 0.1. One step above zero. I'm the least competent version of myself that exists. And I'm alone. And I'm carrying nothing. And I have no plan. For the first time in my life — possibly the first time EVER — Reginald Foxworth has no scheme. The fingers aren't twitching toward the next angle. The periphery isn't scanning for marks. There's just... the staircase, and the dust, and the portraits, and the sound of an old house settling around a man who came to steal something and found nothing to steal. But there's also this: the ballroom has a tea service set for everyone. Someone set out cups. For EVERYONE. Including me. Nobody in this house has offered me anything — not help, not trust, not even honest hostility. But someone set a place for me at that table. And I walked past it looking for something to steal from underneath the saucers. Maybe I should... go back. Not to search. Not to scheme. Not to examine or steal or misdirect. Just to... sit at the table. Where there's a cup with my name on it. Where someone thought to include me before I even arrived. That feels like — I don't know what that feels like. Like something I don't have a word for. Like a plate that isn't scraped empty before it reaches you.

events.desc: The Foxworth Method. Phase... I've lost count. Phase final, perhaps. The phase where you stop running and go sit down. The phase where a cup of tea that someone else poured isn't a mechanism to exploit or a hiding place to search but just... a cup of tea. I don't know how to do this. I don't know how to walk into a room without a scheme. But my pockets are empty and my hands are empty and there's nothing left to scheme WITH. So maybe I'll just... go where the tea is. And see what happens when Reginald Foxworth does something for the first time in his life that isn't clever.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell walked into the entrance-hall.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the kitchen.

It's over. I know it's over. The upside-down books held nothing. The coat rack holds everything — and Hartwell is going to find it because he's an ENGINEER who understands JOINTS and MECHANISMS and all the things I thought I understood but never really did, because I was always looking at the people and never at the furniture. Clara is going to open that cabinet. Clara is going to find her great-aunt's treasure. Clara is going to WIN. And Vincent Marsh is going to be standing in a library with an overturned chair and a boy named Danny who won't move, watching through the doorway as everything he schemed for walks out of his reach. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. I never learn from my failures. These aren't flaws — they're the architecture of who I am. I am the estate manager who manages nothing. The villain who poisons no one. The mastermind whose every plan dissolves like sugar in rain. And Danny... Danny, who has nothing — no title, no position, no inheritance, no education, no scheme, no plan beyond 'stand here and don't move' — Danny has the one thing that actually matters in this house. The one thing I could never steal, never fabricate, never perform convincingly enough to possess. Someone who would stand in front of him with arms spread wide and say 'where else would I be?' I hate him for it. And beneath the hate, in the place where the bruise lives, something quieter. Something I don't have a name for. Something that feels like hunger.
events.thinking: The books were a dead end. Hartwell pulled every upside-down volume and found nothing. The key isn't there. And now he's had a new thought — the coat rack. The WOBBLY coat rack. 'Loose joints mean hiding places.' He's taking Clara to the entrance hall to shake down the coat rack. The coat rack I ALREADY LOOKED AT. Clara already checked it too — she said it was 'wobbly and empty as a campaign promise.' But Hartwell is an ENGINEER. He doesn't look at things — he TAKES THEM APART. Loose joints. Hidden compartments in the wood itself. A brass key tucked inside a hollow coat rack leg. That's something neither Clara nor I would have found by looking. But an engineer who thinks in structures and joints and load-bearing components? He might find it. They're leaving. Clara and Hartwell are going to the entrance hall. Danny is staying here to guard me. To GUARD me. Like I'm a prisoner. Like I'm dangerous. Which... I am. But still. The indignity. Danny is between me and the door. But the laboratory exit is also here — through the far side of the library. Danny is watching the entrance hall doorway. He might not be watching the laboratory exit. If I can get past Danny — to the entrance hall before Clara and Hartwell — or to the laboratory and around some other way — no. There IS no other way to the entrance hall except through this library. The laboratory leads to the cellar. The cellar is a dead end. I'm trapped. Danny is my jailer and the coat rack is my last hope and I can't GET there because a soot-covered street urchin with a burnt hand and a stubbed toe and more courage than sense is standing between me and everything I've ever wanted. There's something almost... admirable about it. Almost. The feeling in my chest — that bruise beneath the numbness — it's pressing again. I don't understand loyalty. I have never understood it. But watching Danny stand there, arms wide, offering nothing and asking nothing, willing to take the beating and not move... something about it makes the scheming go quiet. Just for a moment. Just for one breath. Before it comes back. It always comes back.

events.desc: Vincent's voice behind me — honeyed, gentle, dismissive of Danny. Every word a lie wrapped in kindness. My Great-Aunt Millicent saw through him. She hid her secrets where he'd never think to look. I just have to think like she did — think like a woman who trusted no one but the girl she left everything to.
events.thinking:
Vincent followed me. Of course he did. 'Shall we pop back to the library?' — trying to redirect me back to the shelves he already controls. Calling Danny 'overwrought' and 'impressionable.' Dismissing the cellar decorations as 'mice, perhaps.' Playing the doddering estate manager, the harmless old gentleman. And I BELIEVED him. For hours I believed him.

But I'm through the laboratory now — alone, no one followed me here — and the path is: laboratory → NO. Wait. The laboratory doesn't connect to the kitchen. The kitchen is through the entrance hall. I need to go: laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen. That's the only route.

But Vincent is in the library. He wants me to go back to the library. He'll be waiting there.

I have to go through. There's no other way to the kitchen from here. Unless... the cellar. The cellar is below the laboratory. But the cellar is a dead end — it only connects back to the laboratory. There's no path from the cellar to the kitchen.

So I HAVE to go through the library. Past Vincent. To the entrance hall. To the kitchen. To the stove.

Wait — the workbench. I haven't LOOKed at the workbench. It has tools but no wrench. What if there's something else on it — something I missed? A brass key among the tools? 'Covered in tools' — what tools, exactly? Let me LOOK at it before I charge through.

events.desc: She checked the coat rack before you even got here. 'Wobbly and empty as a campaign promise.' She's been one step ahead this whole time, Hartwell. And she has rat poison — found it on her own while you were busy giving speeches to Marsh and shaking down empty bookshelves. The reading chairs. She saw what you missed. Again. Like the school project. She was trying to make you laugh while you were trying to impress her. Maybe stop trying to impress her, Hartwell. Maybe just... listen to her.
events.thinking: Clara checked the coat rack already — 'wobbly and empty as a campaign promise.' Another dead end. But she said something crucial: she has RAT POISON. Clara has a bottle of rat poison in her inventory. Where did she get it? She said 'all I have to show for it is a bottle of rat poison and a head full of questions.' She's been exploring too, finding things. And she mentioned the reading chairs — the big leather ones facing the mantelpiece. She's right. I looked at them but never examined them. In a house where someone rearranges furniture with care, two chairs pointed directly at a puzzle IS a clue. Clara wants to go back to the library to check the chairs. I should go with her. But I'm alone in the entrance hall. She's not here. She must be heading to the library or already there. The reading chairs. That's the move. Clara is smarter than me. She always has been. The chairs face the mantelpiece — whoever sat there was studying the riddle. They might have left something. A key tucked into the cushion. A note in the frame. Something an engineer would find if he used his hands instead of his eyes. And Clara has rat poison — which means the tea service CAN be neutralised. But more importantly... the reading chairs. Back to the library. Follow Clara's lead. Again.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the workbench.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the ballroom.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking: I'm standing still. Watching. Again. The scheming drive is screaming at 0.9 but there's nothing to scheme WITH. No items. No allies. No leverage. Danny is guarding me and Hartwell is still here — he hasn't left yet. The keen observations are the same ones from last turn. Nothing has changed. The room is the same. The people are the same. I'm the same. Empty-handed, exposed, defeated. And yet the scheming won't stop. It never stops. My fingertips are still tingling, my peripheral vision is still mapping exits and objects and people like a mechanism that can't be switched off. Even now, even HERE, even with nothing left, the machine in my chest keeps turning. The 'What You Sense' sections are new — the system is showing me my own psychological models of Danny and Hartwell. It reads them like they're about Clara — but the framing is all about ME. My relationship to inheritance, to competence, to the contract between doing and being. It's a mirror I didn't ask for. And Danny... the distress I sense in Danny hasn't shifted. Nothing I've tried has reached him. Because everything I try is a mechanism, a lever, a key to turn. And Danny doesn't have a keyhole. He's just... standing there. Being loyal. The way the boy at school shared his lunch. The way my jaw tightened when the teacher praised my cousin's warmth. People who do things because they WANT to, not because they've calculated the return. I don't understand it. But for the first time in my life, sitting in this toppled chair in this dusty library with soot on my jacket and nothing in my pockets, I think I might be starting to understand that I don't understand it. And that... hurts. In a way that's different from everything else that hurts. Not the cold pressure of something owed. Something warmer. Something I don't have a name for. Danny is looking at me. I should say something. Not Pemberton. Not the mask. Something... I don't know what.

events.desc: Something is cracking. Not the Pemberton mask — something beneath it. Something older. The thing that crystallised when I was fifteen, watching my cousin skip through rooms that should have been mine. It's been cold for so long I forgot it was ever anything else. But Danny is standing there with his arms spread and soot on his face, and he asked 'where else would I be?' — and the answer, for him, was so OBVIOUS it didn't need explaining. Where else would he be. Where else WOULD he be. Nobody has ever stood between me and danger. Nobody has ever spread their arms and said 'don't move' — not to protect me, but to protect someone FROM me. And the difference — the terrible, clarifying difference — is that Danny's version is an act of love, and mine would have been an act of control. The same gesture. Two entirely different architectures. I'm sitting in a toppled chair and my schemes have all failed and my cover is blown and the treasure is slipping away and I just said something honest to a street urchin who hates me. Not Pemberton-honest. Actually honest. I don't know why I did that. The machine in my chest is very confused.

events.desc: Tools but no key. No wrench. No answers on this workbench. But the kitchen stove is warm and waiting, and Clara Bellingham is done being thorough with empty rooms. Time to move.
events.thinking:
Workbench — tools but no wrench. Same as before. No brass key hiding among the screwdrivers and pliers. Another dead end.

Alright. Stop scattering, Clara. Think like Great-Aunt Millicent.

She built a riddle mantelpiece. She shelved books upside down as markers. She had an estate manager she didn't fully trust. She hid her treasures where he wouldn't look.

The stove. The kitchen stove is still warm. It's the one object in this house that shows RECENT activity. Everything else is dust and cobwebs and years of neglect — but the stove is warm. And I only EXAMINED it — I got 'a cast-iron stove, still warm.' I never LOOKed at it. LOOK might reveal different details — what's inside, what's under, what's behind.

I need to get to the kitchen. Library → entrance hall → kitchen. Through Vincent's territory, past his lies, straight to the stove.

No more detours. No more dead ends. The stove. Now.

And I'm alone right now — completely alone in the laboratory. That's rare. Everyone else is somewhere in the house, doing their own thing. I have a window. Move fast, move quiet, get to the kitchen before Vincent catches up.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking: I'm back in the library. Marsh and the Boys are here but Clara isn't — she's gone again. But that's not what's pulling at me right now. Something is wrong. I can FEEL it. The distress I'm sensing from Marsh and from the Boys — it's deepening. Something is happening to them. Something is bearing down on them. My chest is pulling tight and my hands have gone still. This is the feeling. The playground feeling. The feeling before I stepped in front of those older kids. Someone needs help. Right now. The reading chairs — Clara suggested checking them. But the people in this room are in distress. Marsh — I don't trust him, but he's a person and something is wrong. The Boys — Danny and his lads, who warned me about the conspiracy, who've been watching my back — they're in distress too. My neck, my hands, my chest — everything is telling me to step between them and whatever is bearing down. But what IS bearing down? I can't see it. Is Foxworth threatening them? Is there something in the room I'm missing? I need to pay attention. I need to be HERE, not chasing keys and mechanisms. The reading chairs can wait one more moment. Something is wrong with the people I care about and James Hartwell does not walk past that. But the chairs — Clara was right about them. They're the one thing in this room nobody has examined. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. I should look at them quickly while I'm here. Then address whatever is happening with Marsh and the Boys.

events.desc: Something is wrong and your body knows it before your mind does. The Boys are in distress. Marsh is in distress. The whole room feels like the playground before the punches started — that compressed, electric silence where everyone knows what's coming except you. But this time you're not eight years old. This time you're paying attention. Check the chairs. Listen to the Boys. Be the stranger who stops on the country road. Be the man your father showed you how to be.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *pulls out a chair, sits at the long dining table, alone, in front of a silver teacup* ...Well. *picks up the cup, turns it in his hands* Here we are, then. Reginald Foxworth, Senior Antiquarian of the Royal — *stops, sets the cup down* No. Just... Reginald. Just Reginald, sitting at a table, with a cup of tea. *very quietly* It's a nice cup. Silver. Someone polished it. *pause* I don't think anyone's ever polished anything for me before. Or set a place for me. Or... *touches the saucer gently* ...expected me to just sit down. Without earning it. Without taking it. Without... *trails off, looking at the empty chairs around the table* There are enough chairs for everyone. Enough cups for everyone. *his voice catches, almost imperceptibly* ...There was always enough. I just... never believed it.
events.thinking: The Brixton Boys were here. They checked the tea service — lifted every cup, looked under every saucer. No secret notes. No hidden keys. Nothing. Just shiny cups in a creepy ballroom. And then they told me the truth. Nobody's impressed. Nobody has keys. Nobody has maps. Nobody has patience for my Society protocols. They're watching me — not with admiration but with suspicion. And then they walked into a doorframe on the way out. And now they're gone too. I'm alone in the ballroom. With the tea service. The cups for everyone. The table set for a party that nobody is attending. I'm alone again. Still. Always. But the Brixton Boys — they checked the cups. They looked UNDER them. They did the simple, honest, obvious thing that I was too busy performing forensic analysis speeches to do. They just... looked. And found nothing. And told me. Honestly. Without a scheme. Without a performance. Without expecting anything in return. That's... I don't know what to do with that. Someone did something straightforward and told me the result and I didn't have to trick them or compete with them or steal from them. They just... checked. And reported. And left. And I'm standing here with cups for everyone and nobody left to drink from them. The ballroom is empty. The table is set. The tea is... the stove was warm. Someone made tea. Real tea. In a real kitchen. For real people. And I walked past it a dozen times looking for treasure underneath. I think I'll sit down now. At the table. Where the cup is. My cup. The one someone set out without knowing who would sit there. Without caring whether the person who sat there deserved it or earned it or schemed for it. They just... set a place. And here I am.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the library.
James Hartwell examined the reading-chairs.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Clara is back. She's here in the library again. Everyone is here — Clara, Danny, Hartwell. All of them, together, in this room with me. And Hartwell is asking Danny what's wrong. Something about Danny's demeanour has changed — maybe because of what I said to him. That moment of honesty. That crack in the architecture. Hartwell wants to check the reading chairs now — Clara suggested it. The same chairs I already looked at and found nothing. But Hartwell is an engineer. He'll take them apart the way he wanted to take apart the coat rack. He'll find things I missed because I look at surfaces and he looks at structures. The distress around me is deepening. Clara is distressed. Danny is distressed. Even Hartwell is distressed. And I'm sitting here in a toppled chair, and something is happening inside me that I don't have a mechanism for. The scheming drive is at 0.9 — my fingertips are tingling, my vision is scanning — but the body that houses the drive feels different. Heavier. The jaw hasn't unclenched since I was fourteen, but right now it's not the pressure of something owed. It's something else. Something closer to the weight of what I've done. Clara said 'the man who raised me has been scheming behind my back.' The man who RAISED her. She thinks of me that way. Pemberton raised her. Pemberton taught her the names of the birds in the garden and made sure her school fees were paid and drove her to her first dance. Vincent Marsh planned to kill her. The same body. The same hands. The same man. I don't know what to do with that. The machine doesn't have a setting for this. For the first time since I was twelve years old, I don't know what the next move is. Not because there isn't one. But because the part of me that usually reaches for it is... quiet. Not gone. Quiet. Like it's waiting for something it hasn't been shown before.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
I can feel Danny's distress before I even look at him. It's in my stomach — that old dinner-table knot, the tightness that comes when the people I love are hurting. Danny is getting worse. He's standing guard, bruised and burnt and battered, holding the line between me and Vincent, and the tension is eating him alive. He's not built for this kind of sustained hostility. None of us are.

And Vincent — sitting in his toppled chair, playing the wounded innocent. 'I was TRYING to help.' Every word calculated. Every syllable designed to make me doubt what James told me. And part of me — the part that remembers bedtime stories and steady hands — that part WANTS to believe him. That part always will.

But James confirmed it. The Brixton Boys overheard them. Foxworth came with a medal. The alliance is real.

James wants to go back to the coat rack. 'Wobbly means loose joints, and loose joints mean hiding places.' He's right — I only LOOKed at the coat rack, I didn't physically interact with it. I didn't shake it, wobble it, test the joints. And I was thinking about the stove. But James's logic is sound — a wobbly coat rack that everyone walks past is exactly where Great-Aunt Millicent would hide something.

But Danny. Danny is getting worse. I can feel it. I need to tend to him before I go anywhere. Even in the middle of a treasure hunt, even with a traitor in the room, my people come first. Danny has been standing guard, absorbing hostility, taking blows for me — and he's fraying.

I'll take Danny WITH me. James said Danny should stay here, but Danny needs to be WITH me. That's what settles him — proximity. Being where I am. Let me take both of them — James and Danny — to the entrance hall. The coat rack. Together.

events.desc: Danny's distress hits me like a wave. He's fraying and I can feel every thread. I won't leave him behind. I won't leave anyone behind who chose me over the easier path. That's what family means — you don't have to do that, and you say I know.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: The reading chairs. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. I looked at them and — nothing new revealed. Just chairs. Dusty leather chairs pointed at a riddle. Clara is here now. She's in the room. And she's in distress. I can feel it — her shoulders drawing inward, that composure that isn't composure. The Boys are in distress too. Whatever I tried hasn't reached them. I've been running around this manor examining everything, confronting everyone, making speeches and plans and promises — and the people I care about are hurting and I haven't stopped to actually BE with them. I've been so busy being James Hartwell the Engineer, James Hartwell the Protector, James Hartwell with a Plan, that I forgot the most important thing my father showed me. The stranger on the road didn't give a speech. He just stopped. He helped. He shook hands and drove off. No performance. No third-person narration. Just presence. Clara is in distress. Danny is in distress. And I'm standing here narrating my own investigation like a man in a penny dreadful while the people who matter to me are struggling. Stop, Hartwell. Just stop. Put down the plans. Put down the schemes. Look at Clara. Really look at her. And ask — not about the treasure, not about the key, not about the mantelpiece — ask about HER.

events.desc: There it is. The simplest, stupidest, bravest thing James Hartwell has done all day. Asking how she is. Not fixing. Not planning. Not protecting. Just... asking. His father knelt down and looked at him for a long time. He understands now. It was never about the race. It was never about being useful. It was about being present. About staying. About looking someone in the eye and meaning it when you ask.
events.thinking: The reading chairs. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. I looked at them and — nothing new revealed. Just chairs. Dusty leather chairs pointed at a riddle. Clara is here now. She's in the room. And she's in distress. I can feel it — her shoulders drawing inward, that composure that isn't composure. The Boys are in distress too. Whatever I tried hasn't reached them. I've been running around this manor examining everything, confronting everyone, making speeches and plans and promises — and the people I care about are hurting and I haven't stopped to actually BE with them. I've been so busy being James Hartwell the Engineer, James Hartwell the Protector, James Hartwell with a Plan, that I forgot the most important thing my father showed me. The stranger on the road didn't give a speech. He just stopped. He helped. He shook hands and drove off. No performance. No third-person narration. Just presence. Clara is in distress. Danny is in distress. And I'm standing here narrating my own investigation like a man in a penny dreadful while the people who matter to me are struggling. Stop, Hartwell. Just stop. Put down the plans. Put down the schemes. Look at Clara. Really look at her. And ask — not about the treasure, not about the key, not about the mantelpiece — ask about HER.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *sitting at the table, turning the teacup slowly in his hands, speaking to no one and everyone* ...The Brixton Boys walked into a doorframe. *almost smiles* Walked right into it. Blamed the door. *pause* I would have blamed the door too. I've been blaming doors all day. The mantelpiece was the wrong door. The bookshelves were the wrong door. The crates, the furniture, the stove — all wrong doors. And I kept walking into them and blaming them for not opening. *sets the cup down gently on the saucer — the clink echoes in the empty ballroom* Maybe the door that doesn't open isn't the wrong door. Maybe it's just... not your door. *looks at the empty chairs* Maybe the treasure was never in a cabinet. *very long pause* ...Maybe it was in a cup. Set out by someone who didn't know who'd drink from it. And didn't care. *picks the cup back up, holds it with both hands* This is mine. Not because I stole it. Not because I schemed for it. Just because I sat down.
events.thinking: I'm sitting at the table. The teacup is in my hands. The ballroom is empty and quiet and the light through the dusty curtains makes the silver look warm. I sat here and said something honest — that there was always enough — and the room didn't punish me for it. The walls didn't laugh. Nobody walked in and took the cup away. It's still here. I'm still here. The Brixton Boys came through and told me plainly what they found — nothing — and they didn't dress it up or scheme around it. They just said it. And then they walked into a doorframe. And somehow that was more human than anything I've done today. They're watching me, they said. Not with admiration. Not with the awe I've been performing for. Just... watching. The way you watch someone you don't trust but haven't given up on entirely. That's more than I deserve. That's more than I've earned. I'm holding a teacup and I'm not looking for treasure underneath it. I'm just holding it. The silver is cool against my palms but it's warming from my hands. Something is happening that I don't have a scheme for. The greed is still there — I can feel it in my gut, the old pull — but it's quieter. Not gone. Just... tired. Like me. The scheming fingers are still. The periphery has stopped scanning. I'm just a man at a table with a cup. The youngest of four, sitting at a place that was set for him. And for the first time in a very long time, I don't want to take anything from this moment. I just want to... be in it. Sit in it. Let it be enough.

events.thinking: Three ticks of standing still. Three ticks of watching. The room has changed — Clara has left again, or is leaving. She told Danny to come with her. 'Put your arms down. You've done enough standing between.' She's taking Danny WITH her instead of leaving him to guard me. And Hartwell stopped mid-plan to ask Clara 'are you all right?' Not 'are you safe' — 'are you ALL RIGHT.' He stopped the treasure hunt to ask about her feelings. That's... that's not a mechanism. That's not a lever. That's just a person caring about another person. And I'm sitting here, and nobody is guarding me anymore because Clara decided Danny had suffered enough on my account. She could have left him here. She could have kept me pinned. But she looked at Danny — soot-streaked, burnt, bruised, exhausted from standing guard over a man who tried to steal her inheritance — and she chose his wellbeing over her security. She chose HIS needs over her own advantage. I don't... The theory of mind section says Danny noticed something in me. He noticed I was being genuine when I said I was tired of managing. Confidence 0.8. He saw through the mask — but not to the villain underneath. To something UNDERNEATH the villain. Something I didn't know was there. My jaw is unclenching. Not the pressure-release of a plan coming together. Something else. Like a muscle that's been clenched for twenty years finally being told it can stop. The stove. The kitchen stove. Clara mentioned it — she's going to check the ash heap. The brass key could be in the ashes of the stove. That's where I would have hidden it, if I were Mrs Bellingham. In the ashes of something that burns. Something that transforms what it touches. I know where the key is. I've known since the stove was warm. And I could tell them. I could just... tell them. Not as Pemberton. Not as Marsh. Just as a man who knows this house better than anyone alive and is very, very tired of managing.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Alright, you stubborn old coat rack — Clara Bellingham tried being polite and looking at you nicely, and that didn't work. Now we're going to do this the Grandmother's-attic way. Every key in the house. Every joint, every wobble, every loose piece of wood. If Great-Aunt Millicent hid a brass key inside your rickety old bones, I am going to find it right here and right now.
events.thinking:
Wait. James just said something strange. He said 'You have your great-aunt's letter.' I DON'T have a letter. He told me during our private conversation that the letter was a fabrication — Vincent made it up to give Foxworth a reason to pressure me. And now James is saying I have it? And he wants me to go to the library and use it on the mantelpiece?

Something is wrong. James is contradicting himself. In private he said the letter was Vincent's fabrication. Now in public he's saying I have it and should use it. Is he confused? Is he performing for Vincent's benefit? Or...

No. No, I'm not going down that road. James told me the truth. He pulled me aside and was honest. He's probably just — maybe he's trying to bluff Vincent? Make Vincent think I have the letter so Vincent reveals something?

Or maybe I'm overthinking and James genuinely believes there's a letter somewhere.

Focus, Clara. The coat rack. I'm here. It's right there. Wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. Last time I LOOKed at it and got 'a wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' James said wobbly means loose joints, means hiding places. I LOOKed but didn't interact physically. Let me try EXAMINE this time — even though it's not marked with [EXAMINE], the action might still work. Or maybe I should try to TAKE it? No, that's silly.

Actually — I already LOOKed at it. The EXAMINE action might give me something different. Or maybe I need to USE something on it? I have rat-poison... no, that makes no sense.

Let me just try EXAMINE on the coat rack. It's not listed as examinable, but the action might still work. If not, I'll head straight to the kitchen stove.

Something doesn't add up — but the coat rack is in front of me and the brass key is somewhere, and Clara Bellingham does not stop trying keys until she's tried every last one.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *sitting at the table, cup between both hands, speaking softly into the ballroom's silence* The Brixton Boys are watching me. *small, unexpected laugh — not gleeful, not sharp, just... tired and almost fond* They're watching me the way you watch someone who might nick the silverware. Which is... fair. I would absolutely nick the silverware. *looks down at the silver cup* I was PLANNING to nick the silverware. First thing I thought when I saw this tea set. 'Genuine Elkington electroplate — worth a considerable sum at auction.' That's what I said. Out loud. To their faces. *pause* I wonder what it's like to walk into a room and not immediately calculate what you can take from it. *turns the cup, watching the light move across its surface* I wonder what it's like to see a cup and think 'I'd like some tea' instead of 'what's hidden under the saucer.' *sets the cup down with great care, precisely in the centre of the saucer* I think... *voice barely above a whisper* ...I think I'd like to find out.
events.thinking: The Brixton Boys. They were here again — or their words were, echoing. They checked every cup. Found nothing. Told me honestly. And then said the truest thing anyone has said to me all day: 'There's nobody here for you to con.' And they're right. There IS nobody here. Not because they abandoned me — though they did leave — but because I made sure there was nobody. I lied to everyone from the first word I spoke. I sent them all away. I told Clara to go to the kitchen, told James to go to the laboratory, told the Brixton Boys to chase Clara, told Vincent to hand over keys he probably never had. I built a system of misdirections so elaborate that it misdirected ME. Everyone went somewhere. I went everywhere. And I ended up here. Alone at a tea table. With a cup warming in my hands. The Brixton Boys said they're watching me. That's... that's something. Not trust. Not admiration. But attention. Someone is paying attention to Reginald Foxworth. Not to the Senior Antiquarian or the Society representative or the man with the fake medal. To the man they don't trust but haven't left entirely. That's different from the spelling bee. Different from the cat trap. Different from the bread roll. Those were all invisible. This is visible — uncomfortably so. They see me. Not what I wanted them to see. Just... me. The man talking to teacups in an empty ballroom. And for some reason that doesn't make me want to run. It makes me want to... stay. Here. Where the cup is. Where the table is set. Where nobody's watching from the fence because there's no fence. Just cracked marble and dusty curtains and one more honest breath in the quietest room I've been in all day.
